5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs. The growth *extract* stage converts each **new**
9	lesson down the promotion ladder; this pass sweeps the **existing** prose backlog for rules that
10	are always-testable but still live only as prose — and converts them, so the packs keep shedding
11	context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is first learned. It runs as
12	grow_with_claudinite's daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` task, and on demand.
13	
14	## Scope — the pack paths you were given
15	
16	Work only the **pack paths configured for this repo** (the task passes them in its Context): a
17	consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
18	improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21	
22	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
36	
37	## How to convert one
38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Trim the prose** to rationale — the check owns enforcement now; leaving both pays twice and
50	   springs the drift trap.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
55	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
56	check to the same fixture bar.
57	
58	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the

1	# Checks — deterministic enforcement of the corpus (design)
2	
3	> **Status: implemented** (issue #127, #131). The runner, the baseline + technology packs, Stop
4	> hook, PreToolUse guard, and the pack-prose loader are live; the corpus is reorganized into
5	> `packs/` (prose + checks, active by declaration) and `skills/` (activity-scoped procedures).
6	> This doc is the rationale and the ongoing design record. The per-rule audit lives in
7	> [docs/conversion-inventory.md](../../docs/conversion-inventory.md).
8	
9	## The problem
10	
11	The corpus enforces style/practice rules as instructions. Instructions have three standing costs:
12	
13	1. **Context** — the always-on baseline loads every session whether or not it's needed, and
14	   adherence degrades as loaded context grows.
15	2. **Silent trigger failure** — soft-loaded docs depend on the agent following their trigger
16	   ("read filePlacement.md before placing a file"), which is itself instruction-following that
17	   fails silently. A rule the agent didn't read can't help.
18	3. **Invisible obsolescence** — a rule a newer Claude Code follows by default keeps costing
19	   tokens and attention forever; nothing measures that it stopped earning its place.
20	
21	A deterministic check inverts all three: it costs zero context until violated, fires whether or
22	not anything was read, and its firing history is measurable — a check that never fails is
23	evidence its rule can retire.
24	
25	## Why this is the right mechanism
26	
27	Anthropic's published guidance says this directly: hooks exist to provide "deterministic control
28	… ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them"
29	(hooks guide); CLAUDE.md is "context, not enforced" (memory doc); and the core best-practice is
30	"give Claude a check it can run … Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and
31	iterates until the check passes" (best practices). The corpus already states the principle in
32	an agent-practices skill: *"Prose is a request; the
33	post-hoc diff check is the guarantee."* This design scales that sentence up.
34	
35	## What converts — and what doesn't
36	
37	An instruction leaves context only when a deterministic mechanism can carry it. Four targets,
38	picked per rule:
39	
40	| Mechanism | Fits when | Examples from the corpus |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **Post-hoc check** (this system) | The rule constrains the *state of the repo* after work | file placement, dangling references, workflow lint, lifecycle compliance |
43	| **PreToolUse hook** | The action must be blocked *before* it runs | never delete a remote branch; don't `issue_write`-overwrite an issue body |
44	| **Skill / script** | A *procedure* or *knowledge* with a nameable (or path-scoped) trigger | the merge recipe; the lessons pass; the technology gotcha files |
45	| **Platform setting** | The platform enforces it outright, for free | squash-only merges; branch protection |
46	
47	Two classes deliberately **stay as instructions**:
48	
49	- **Process/judgment rules** — problem-first consensus, bug investigation method, naming
50	  quality. They shape work *in flight* and leave no artifact a check can inspect. Converting
51	  them post-hoc would also catch violations only after the expensive rework they exist to
52	  prevent.
53	- **Platform-gotcha knowledge** (`technologies/`) — split **per gotcha**, by whether the bad
54	  pattern has a *static signature in the artifact*. Where it does, it converts to a tech-pack
55	  check — a SAM `Handler` still carrying the entry's subdirectory under an esbuild build, an
56	  esbuild declared in `devDependencies`, a `SetIcon({path: …})`, a CloudFront custom
57	  origin-request policy listing `Authorization` — and the agent never needs to know the gotcha
58	  in advance: writing the bad pattern fails the check in the same session, moving discovery
59	  from runtime (often the first deploy or invoke) to write-time, with the gotcha's teaching in
60	  the failure message. Only the signature-less residue stays as skill knowledge: runtime
61	  divergence invisible in the artifact (jsdom *behaving* unlike Chrome, CORS being decided
62	  server-side) and diagnostic know-how. The release pack's **contract** is the
63	  largest signature-rich case — a conformance suite waiting to be written.
64	
65	## Architecture
66	
67	```
68	packs/                        # the mounted corpus: prose + checks, active by declaration
69	  registry.mjs                #   structural discovery — any packs/<name>/pack.mjs is a pack
70	  load-active-prose.mjs       #   SessionStart hook: emits active packs' RULES.md
71	  <baseline>/                 #   the baseline: RULES.md + the core checks (declared like any pack)
72	  <technology>/               #   coding gotchas (RULES.md, prose only)
73	  <technology>-release/       #   RELEASE.md (standard) + stubs + conformance checks (opt-in)
74	  <technology>/               #   the workflow lints (no prose)
75	  <technology>/  <technology>/  …      # more prose-only tech packs
76	  <project-class>/            #   a project-class pack (prose-only, declared)
77	checks/                       # the ENGINE only (runs the packs' checks)
78	  run.mjs                     #   dependency-free Node CLI
79	  lib/                        #   git diff scoping, findings format, markdown + manifest helpers
80	  stop-hook.mjs               #   blocks the agent's stop on blocking findings
81	  pretooluse-guard.mjs        #   blocks forbidden actions before they run
82	  test/                       #   fixtures (scratch git repos), red-first
83	packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/   # activity-scoped procedures, bundled in their owning pack
84	  checks.mjs                  #   the test-the-world checks that validate this skill's action
85	```
86	
87	**Skill-owned checks.** A skill defines the performance of an *action*; the test-the-world
88	check that validates that action's result belongs **beside the SKILL.md that defines it**, not
89	in a pack that owns none of the context. So a skill may carry its own checks — the
90	`routine-structure` check lives in its owning skill's folder, next to the routine-authoring
91	prose it enforces, with its test co-located too. A skill lives inside its owning pack
92	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/` — #385), so discovery IS the pack registry: any bundled skill's
93	`checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) is gathered onto the pack (`skillChecks`) and
94	runs when the pack is active. The pack gate only says the project opted into the pack — not
95	that this skill's action ever happened in this repo — so a skill check's `run` must still
96	**detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and return `[]` when
97	the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing before it asserts
98	anything). Get that wrong and the check fires false findings on every unrelated repo the corpus
99	is mounted in. Reserve skill checks for the world-state a skill's action leaves behind; a rule
100	with no skill to anchor it stays a baseline check.
101	
102	**Where a check goes — the litmus test.** Classify by what the checked *artifact* is, not by
103	which doc teaches the fix (the `doc` pointer is where you *learn* the remedy — most baseline
104	checks point at a skill, so it is **not** the classifier):
105	
106	- present in ~every repo (markdown links, file layout, the root `CLAUDE.md`, git history, a
107	  branch's issue reference) → a **baseline** check;
108	- present only when a declared **technology** is (a workflow, a SAM template, the release
109	  stubs) → a **technology-pack** check, whose relevance is gated by declaration;
110	- present **only because one skill's discrete action created it** (a routine folder, from
111	  authoring a routine) → a **skill** check.
112	
113	Only the third — *the artifact would not exist had the action never run* — earns a home in the
114	skill. `routine-structure` is the sole current case: a routine folder exists only because
115	someone authored a routine. `squash-merge-history` points at the merge skill but stays
116	in the baseline, because git history exists in every repo and is disturbed by any merge, not only that
117	skill's action; `claude-md-length`, `generated-merge-driver`, and the placement check likewise
118	inspect artifacts every repo has, so they stay in the baseline despite naming a skill in `doc`.
119	
120	**Not every pack-machinery concern is a check.** The `.claudinite-checks.json` *settings* are
121	validated when the file loads, not by a conformance rule: malformed JSON, an unknown property,
122	and an unknown pack name are equally settings errors, surfaced by the runner as blocking `config`
123	findings. A pack's `marker` only *suspects* the pack is wanted — whether to declare it is the
124	project's call — so nothing checks that a declared pack carries its marker, or that a marker's
125	pack is declared. Pack **dependencies** (`requires`) are likewise resolved when the declaration is
126	*written* — bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill run `resolveDeclaredPacks` to pull each
127	declared pack's transitive `requires` into the file, materializing the prerequisite (like
128	the baseline) rather than nagging at every Stop. A materialized dependency is written as
129	`{ "id": ..., "via": [...] }` — `via` naming the declared packs that require it — so the file
130	itself records why the dependency is there.
131	
132	**Runner contract.** `node .claudinite/checks/run.js`. Dependency-free Node — no `npm install`
133	step exists on the tarball mount, and the corpus's own "earn each dependency" rule applies to
134	us first. Exit 0 = clean, exit 1 = blocking findings. The default scope is the **whole repo**:
135	on a text corpus the full sweep costs milliseconds, and only full scope sees cross-file
136	breakage — a change in one file dangling a reference in an unchanged one. The steady state is
137	a repo at zero findings (or reviewed acceptances), held there by every run. `--changed`
138	(diff vs the merge-base with main) exists only as a transitional aid while adopting a repo
139	that carries a backlog — it is not the enforcement default. (Rules that are inherently about
140	the *delta* — new suppression markers, commits referencing an issue — diff against the
141	merge-base in either scope.)
142	
143	**Pack selection: declared for deterministic execution, fingerprinted against drift.** The
144	packs a project runs are **pinned in `.claudinite-checks.json`**
145	(`"packs": ["baseline", "a-technology-pack", "a-release-pack"]`; no pack runs
146	undeclared — the baseline too is declared explicitly, seeded by bootstrap).
147	Execution is a closed, declared set: every rule in a declared pack
148	runs when its scope's surface runs — the work rules at the Stop hook, the world rules in the
149	test/CI flow — with no inference at execution time, so "the
150	project uses technology X" deterministically implies "every X check ran." Bootstrap writes the
151	initial declaration from the repo's fingerprint — a pack's `detect` marker (`.github/workflows/`
152	→ a workflow-lint pack; a `manifest.json` with `manifest_version` → the extension packs; the
153	release-workflow `name:`s → the conformance suite) seeds it at `--init`. But a marker only
154	*suspects* a pack is wanted: from then on the declaration is authoritative, and whether to add a
155	newly adopted technology's pack, or drop one whose technology has left, is the **project's** call
156	— the checker never second-guesses it. What *is* enforced is settings **validity**: an unknown
157	pack name, an unknown property, or malformed JSON is caught when the file loads
158	(`loadConfig` + the runner) and surfaced as a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as
159	much a settings error as bad JSON. `.claudinite-checks.json` additionally holds per-rule
160	**overrides** and **acceptances** — at the top level for project-wide decisions, or on a pack's
161	own entry for the ones that pack's declaration motivates (see engine/checks/README.md).
162	
163	A declared id may name a **canon** pack or one of the repo's **own local packs**
164	(`.claudinite/local_packs/<id>/` — the project's tracked, project-specific packs, discovered from
165	the repo's own tree alongside the mounted canon; canonically declared by the namespaced token
166	`local_packs/<id>`, the bare id accepted while the fleet migrates — see engine/checks/README.md). Both
167	are the same closed-declared-set execution;
168	`knownIds` spans both, so a local id is valid, not an unknown-pack error, while a broken or
169	id-colliding local `pack.mjs` is surfaced as a blocking `config` finding rather than silently
170	dropping the pack's checks. A local pack's checks run when it is declared, exactly like a canon
171	pack's; this is where a project's *own* deterministic rules live (the checks-over-prose economy,
172	applied at the project's level) instead of always-loaded prose.
173	
174	**Acceptances are the escape hatch — deterministic and reviewable.** Rules with judgment
175	exemptions (a placement rule's "deliberate cross-cutting concern") need a way to say "yes, on
176	purpose" that isn't a fight with the hook: a per-finding `accept` entry with a mandatory reason
177	string, keyed by rule id + path. It lands in the diff like any code, so the *decision* gets
178	reviewed once instead of re-litigated every session. An acceptance a pack's adoption forces
179	lives on that pack's `packs` entry, so its provenance — which declaration required which
180	exception — is the file's own structure.
181	
182	An acceptance is a **check-the-world** instrument: a persistent, committed exemption a future
183	sweep keeps re-finding and must be told to ignore. It is the wrong tool for a **check-the-work**
184	finding — a conversation- or branch-scoped rule (e.g. `feature-requirements-first`) whose finding
185	a fresh session wouldn't even re-raise; accepting one leaves a permanent suppression for a
186	one-session artifact. Author a check-the-work rule to be **satisfiable by fixing the work, or to
187	self-skip** when its precondition isn't met (the spec it enforces against isn't in the repo, say):
188	a finding no correct work can clear forces the wrong remedy — an accept, or a post-hoc rebase —
189	so it's a bug in the rule, not a candidate for an acceptance.
190	
191	And when a rule mandates an **ordering** — X must happen before Y — it ships with a
192	check-the-work verification of that order, judged on the surface where the order is visible:
193	the conversation transcript (`feature-requirements-first`'s comment-scoped doc-first ordering)
194	or the branch commit log (a rule-before-fix test asserting the outlawing commit is an ancestor
195	of the fixing one, `pack-independence`'s pattern). A stated ordering with no check-the-work
196	verifier is prose-only enforcement — exactly what this system exists to replace.
197	
198	**The finding is the instruction.** This is the context economy of the whole design: the rule's
199	teaching text moves out of always-loaded context and into the failure message, paying its token
200	cost only on violation, in the session that violated it, pointed at the exact spot. Every
201	finding carries: rule id, `file:line`, what's wrong, *why* (one line — the model generalizes
202	from motivation), the fix, and a doc pointer for depth.
203	
204	<example>
205	
206	```
207	reference-distance  src/report/render.js:12
208	  imports ../../util/dates.js at distance 4.
209	  Why: the folder tree should encode the dependency graph; far reaches make it lie.
210	  Fix: move dates.js next to its users, lift it to a common ancestor, or accept it
211	       in .claudinite-checks.json with a reason if it's a deliberate cross-cutting util.
212	  More: .claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
213	```
214	
215	</example>
216	
217	## Enforcement wiring
218	
219	The two scopes fire at **different times**, because they answer different questions. The *work*
220	scope judges the change in front of the session and belongs on a per-turn hook; the *world* scope
221	is a whole-repo invariant assertion — the same shape as a test suite — and belongs wherever the
222	project runs its tests, not on every turn.
223	
224	**Work scope: a Stop hook is the guarantee; instructions are not.** Bootstrap registers one hook
225	in the consumer's `.claude/settings.json` (the same mechanism as the existing SessionStart hooks):
226	
227	1. The Stop hook fires when the agent finishes a turn.
228	2. It **fast-exits in milliseconds** when no tracked file differs from `main` — conversational
229	   turns cost nothing.
230	3. Otherwise it runs the **work** sweep (`check_the_work.mjs`, with the session transcript); on
231	   findings it exits 2 with them on stderr. Claude Code blocks the stop and feeds that text back
232	   to the agent, which fixes the violations **in the same session**. A clean run stops silently.
233	
234	Loop safety comes from convergence (fixed findings stop firing) plus Claude Code's own runaway
235	protection (it overrides a Stop hook after ~8 consecutive blocks).
236	
237	**World scope: wired into the project's test/CI flow (revises #385).** The whole-repo sweep runs
238	as its own step wherever the project runs its tests — a CI job, a `make test` target, an npm
239	script — invoked as the standalone `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`
240	command. It is deliberately **not** a language-specific test file (a `*.test.mjs` a Node runner
241	discovers): a Python/Rust/Go consumer's suite could not load one, and the sweep is the engine's
242	own always-vendored Node CLI, so it runs as a step in any flow regardless of the project's
243	language. Bootstrap wires this step during adoption, adding a minimal flow where the repo has
244	none. This **supersedes the original #385 decision** ("the Stop hook is the whole enforcement
245	surface; consumers ship no CI job"): the earlier design kept the world sweep on Stop to spare
246	consumers a CI setup, but running a whole-repo sweep every turn is work misplaced in time, and a
247	human editing on GitHub web (or any non-session tool) is now caught by the test/CI flow the
248	change lands through rather than by the next session's Stop.
249	
250	**The conversation surface (Stop hook only).** Some process rules leave their artifact not in
251	the repo but in the *session itself* — e.g. `comment-classification` (the reply to the owner's
252	latest comment must declare an explicit `Comment class:` line: the assessment stays judgment,
253	but that an assessment was made is checkable) and `feature-requirements-first` (a
254	feature-classified comment's doc-first ordering on the branch). The Stop hook is the one surface
255	that can carry these: Claude Code passes the hook `transcript_path` on stdin, the hook forwards
256	it as `--transcript`, and `ctx.conversation()` exposes the parsed session
257	([helpers/session-transcript.mjs](helpers/session-transcript.mjs)). Everywhere else — CI, a manual run — the transcript
258	is absent and these rules self-gate to `[]`, the same self-supplied relevance gate skill checks
259	use. Two scoping choices keep them convergent rather than nagging: only the *latest* owner
260	comment is judged (a transcript is append-only, so an old omission could never be fixed), and
261	the ordering rule scopes to commits after the comment's timestamp (earlier work on the branch is
262	never re-litigated). The Stop hook's clean fast path also means a purely conversational turn —
263	no tracked change vs the base — runs no checks at all, conversation rules included.
264	
265	**Prefer a platform setting when one exists — but never trust it.** Squash-only merging is a
266	GitHub repo setting; force-push protection is branch protection. The setting does the
267	*enforcing*, but it's configuration like any other: it can be off, get switched off, or be
268	bypassed, and nothing notices. So every setting rung pairs with a check that verifies it, in
269	order of strength:
270	
271	- **Effect check (preferred)** — offline and deterministic, it verifies the *outcome* the
272	  setting guarantees rather than the setting itself: squash-only ⇒ the change lands squashed,
273	  so its own commits carry no merge commit (`squash-merge-history` in the baseline pack). It
274	  is scoped to the work — the merge commits the current change introduces on HEAD's first-parent
275	  chain since the merge-base — not the repo's whole history: it catches the setting being off or
276	  bypassed *for this change* without re-auditing (and demanding acceptances for) legacy merges
277	  already on `main` that the work never touched. Testing the work, not the world, is what keeps
278	  the check from firing on every unrelated session.
279	
280	  **A work-scoped rule is only as honest as the ref it scopes against.** "Since the merge-base"
281	  is a correct definition that silently becomes a wrong verdict when the base ref is stale —
282	  a cloud session's clone freezes `origin/main` at container-creation time, so everything the
283	  base branch gained since then reads as introduced by the work, and a *blocking* rule starts
284	  reporting other people's merges on a branch that has none of its own. Two mechanisms keep the
285	  scope honest, both in `buildContext` rather than in any one rule: the base ref is refreshed
286	  before the merge-base is computed (best-effort, bounded, opt-out — [README](README.md)), and
287	  candidates are confirmed against the base ref itself, because `git merge-base` returns one of
288	  several equally-good answers on a criss-cross history and the one it picks can leave a merge
289	  that is already on the base branch inside the range. Scoping a delta rule is two jobs: pick
290	  the range, and make sure the range's endpoint is telling the truth.
291	- **Config check** — reads the setting via the platform API and fails when it's off. Needs a
292	  network-capable surface: rules carry a surface tag, the Stop hook runs only offline rules,
293	  CI runs what its repo token can read (e.g. the allow-merge-commit flags), and the fleet
294	  maintenance routine covers settings a repo token can't (e.g. branch protection). Follow-up
295	  work alongside the Phase 2 packs.
296	
297	## Governance
298	
299	- **A converted rule leaves its doc.** The check's failure message owns the rule now; the doc
300	  keeps only rationale and the judgment parts. Keeping both pays twice and springs the corpus's
301	  own drift trap (two sources of truth).
302	- **Fail fast: a new check ships at its real severity — blocking for defect-kind rules.** A
303	  wrong blocking check surfaces in the very next session and gets fixed; an advisory false
304	  positive is noise nobody reads, so a burn-in stage never actually observes the precision it
305	  waits for. The escape hatches bound a bad check's blast radius: a reasoned acceptance, a
306	  severity override, and the Stop hook's own two-block release. `advisory` remains a per-rule
307	  **kind**, not a stage — for rules whose own semantics are directional (a placement rule's
308	  metric is "a direction, not a hard gate"), where a finding is a smell to judge, not a defect
309	  to fix. Revisit delayed adoption only if the fleet grows people who can be hurt by a wrong
310	  block.
311	- **Telemetry drives retirement.** The runner logs firings; the fleet-maintenance routine
312	  already reads every vendored repo and can report "rules that never fired in N days" —
313	  obsolescence made measurable, the property instructions never had.
314	
315	## Skills — the on-demand layer for what checks can't carry
316	
317	Checks carry the *enforceable* rules. Everything else that today rides on soft pointers —
318	procedures, task-gated practices, technology knowledge — moves to **Agent Skills**, a mechanism
319	the system doesn't use yet. The docs' own decision rule fits exactly: *"Create a skill when …
320	a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact"*, and knowledge-bearing
321	skills are explicitly endorsed (*"reference content adds knowledge … conventions, patterns,
322	style guides, domain knowledge"*). The official hook-vs-skill line mirrors this design's ladder:
323	*"Use a hook when the action must happen the same way every time … Use a skill when Claude
324	should decide how to apply the steps, or when the content is knowledge rather than a script."*
325	
326	**What a skill buys over a CLAUDE.md soft pointer.** The token economics are roughly neutral —
327	a skill's name + description sit in context every session (progressive disclosure: the body
328	loads only on invocation), about what an index line costs today. The real gain is **trigger
329	reliability**: today a `tasks/` doc helps only if the agent remembers to follow the index line
330	("read before writing a test") — an instruction-following step that fails silently. Skill
331	matching is harness-managed and trained-for, skills are user-invocable as `/name` too (manual
332	invocation is deterministic — it runs when typed), and technology skills can be
333	**`paths`-scoped** (glob frontmatter) so they surface exactly when the matching files are
334	touched — a structural trigger, not a remembered one.
335	
336	Be clear about what this is *not*: **model-invocation of a skill is still probabilistic** —
337	better odds than a soft pointer, never a guarantee. That is precisely why this design's
338	division of labor puts nothing that *must* happen on a skill: enforcement lives in hooks,
339	checks, and settings, which are deterministic by construction; skills carry only guidance whose
340	worst-case miss is today's status quo. In particular, check execution never depends on skill
341	routing — the Stop hook runs the declared packs whether or not any skill fired. The split is
342	therefore **per-rule, not per-doc**: a doc's enforceable rules go to a pack (which runs
343	unconditionally for every project that declares it), its judgment residue rides the skill, and
344	there is deliberately no one-to-one correspondence between an instruction file and a pack. Two documented limits
345	to respect: keep descriptions tight (the listing truncates them, and the description budget
346	scales with the context window — many verbose skills degrade matching), and keep each
347	`SKILL.md` body well under 500 lines.
348	
349	### The catalog
350	
351	There is no skill catalog (#385): a skill is its owning pack's content
352	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the pack's own README names what it bundles, and the
353	harness surfaces skills by their frontmatter descriptions, which is the routing.
354	
355	What stays always-loaded after this: a trimmed
356	baseline `RULES.md`, the judgment core of
357	the agent-practices skill (its trigger — "writing
358	code" — is near-universal, so a skill gains little; revisit with telemetry), and a much smaller
359	index. The routing index largely dissolves: routing *is what skill descriptions do natively*.
360	
361	### Delivery — incremental now, plugin end-state
362	
363	- **Now (works with both mount methods):** each skill is bundled in its owning pack
364	  (`<pack>/skills/<name>/`), and the SessionStart hook `engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`
365	  regenerates `.claude/skills/<name>` symlinks for the active packs' union each session —
366	  nothing committed (a committed link dangles on every plain checkout). Symlinked skill
367	  directories are documented, supported behavior, and skill changes are picked up live within
368	  a session — so mounts generated at session start still land, the same property the tarball
369	  sync populating their targets already relies on.
370	- **Later, maybe — Claudinite as a plugin (contingent on a spike).** A plugin is nothing
371	  exotic: a directory layout inside an ordinary git repo (`skills/`, `commands/`,
372	  `hooks/hooks.json`, a `plugin.json` manifest) plus a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` that
373	  lets the repo serve as its own catalog. **No publication to Anthropic** — any git repo works
374	  as a marketplace directly, and the repo may carry arbitrary other content alongside the
375	  plugin dirs, so Claudinite would remain exactly the freely-amended GitHub repo it is (growth
376	  PRs, this doc, everything — unchanged). The draw: plugins bundle precisely this design's
377	  pieces — skills, commands, and hooks (SessionStart, Stop, PreToolUse) with bundled scripts
378	  addressable via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — and a consumer repo can commit
379	  `extraKnownMarketplaces` + `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json` to enable it for
380	  everyone. **Why it is not the plan of record:** the docs leave the operational questions that
381	  matter most to this system unanswered — how promptly consumers receive updates (manual
382	  `/plugin marketplace update` is documented; session-start auto-refresh is not), whether
383	  web/cloud sessions load marketplace plugins at all, and whether plugin hooks behave
384	  identically to settings-registered ones. A daily-growth corpus lives or dies on update
385	  latency, and the current SessionStart tarball sync *guarantees* latest-`main` every session.
386	  So: phases 1–4 ship entirely on the existing mount + symlinks and depend on the plugin route
387	  for nothing; adopt it only if a Phase-5 spike proves same-day propagation, web support, and
388	  hook parity. (Also documented: a plugin cannot inject always-on CLAUDE.md-style prose, so the
389	  residual baseline keeps its `@`-import either way.)
390	
391	## Growth pipeline: checks-first promotion
392	
393	New lessons enter the canon through the growth lifecycle (extract → promote → dedup). Today
394	the promote step generalizes a lesson and routes it to a prose doc.
395	Under this design, **prose becomes the fallback, not the default** — the point of promotion is
396	to relieve every project's context, and a check relieves it completely while prose only
397	relocates it.
398	
399	**The promotion ladder.** Every lesson that clears the worthiness bar is triaged down the same
400	mechanism order as the conversion table above — the *first* rung that can carry it wins:
401	
402	1. **Platform setting** — the platform enforces it outright, always paired with the check
403	   that verifies it holds (effect check first, config check where a token can read it).
404	2. **PreToolUse hook** — a bad action to block before it runs.
405	3. **Post-hoc check** — a constraint on repo state.
406	4. **Skill** — a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger.
407	5. **Prose canon** — only for what none of the above can carry, and the landing **names its
408	   reason** (judgment / in-flight behavior / platform knowledge), logged per lesson in the
409	   promote tracking issue so conversion rates are auditable.
410	
411	Concretely, three growth docs change:
412	
413	- **`item-routing.md`** gains a step 0: *mechanism triage*
414	  before file routing. "Which doc owns this" is only asked for lessons that fall through to
415	  rung 5.
416	- **the promote task doc**: for a rung-3 lesson, the routine authors
417	  the check in the same PR — rule id, detection, the failure message (which *is* the
418	  generalized lesson text), **plus a fixture proving it fires** on a violating input and stays
419	  quiet on a clean one (see-it-fail applies to checks too). When it can't produce a confident
420	  detection + fixture, it lands the lesson as prose **and** opens a tagged conversion-backlog
421	  issue — a visible miss to sweep later, never a silently-shipped broken check.
422	- **the dedup task doc**: a canon **check** covers a local prose item the
423	  same way a canon line does — better, since the coverage is enforced rather than stated. The
424	  runner exposes the rule catalog machine-readably (`run.js --list`: rule id, description,
425	  failure message, doc pointer); dedup quotes a **rule id** where it today quotes a canon line.
426	  This answers the obvious worry — "the canon won't have the instruction, only a test": the
427	  check *carries* its instruction as data (its failure message), so dedup compares against the
428	  catalog exactly as it compares against prose today, and more mechanically, since rule ids are
429	  stable where prose wording drifts. The keep-test is unchanged: a local item that says *more*
430	  than the check detects (a stronger point about a narrower case) stays.
431	
432	Extract is untouched: project-local capture stays prose at the project's own level —
433	conversion is a promotion-time judgment, made once, centrally.
434	
435	## Phasing
436	
437	1. **Runner + Stop hook + first baseline checks** — reference-integrity, task-lifecycle,
438	   warning-suppression (blocking); the placement check (advisory by kind). Bootstrap gains the
439	   hook-registration step.
440	2. **a workflow-lint pack + a release-conformance pack**, piloted on one
441	   extension repo.
442	3. **Baseline restructure** — the first skills (a merge recipe, a lessons pass) + the
443	   squash-only setting; temporary-workarounds → PreToolUse hook; slim the converted docs and
444	   the index.
445	4. **Skills layer + growth pivot** — the rest of the corpus (practice + technology skills,
446	   symlink delivery in bootstrap), and the promotion ladder lands in
447	   the promote task doc,
448	   `item-routing.md`, and
449	   the dedup task doc.
450	5. **(Contingent) plugin packaging** — only after a spike proves same-day update propagation,
451	   web-session support, and hook parity; until then the mount + symlink delivery is the plan of
452	   record and nothing depends on this phase.
453	6. **(Deferred)** LLM-judge checks in CI for judgment rules (naming, comment quality) —
454	   possible, but nondeterministic and token-costly; revisit only after 1–4 prove out.

1 # HTML 2 3 Portable, project-agnostic practices for hand-authored HTML — semantic markup, accessibility, forms, and the document structure pitfalls that recur regardless of framework — true for any HTML read cold. 4 5 - **Injected block markup inside a `

` silently empties it — read the sibling, not the tag.** When a `

` is filled with raw HTML (e.g. `innerHTML`, or a framework's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` / `v-html` / `ng-bind-html`), a block element inside it (a `

`, etc.) is disallowed by the HTML content model, so the parser (browser or jsdom, same rule) auto-closes the `

` right before it and the injected content lands as the `

`'s **next sibling**. Read `element.nextElementSibling`. 6 - **An ambiguous numeric slash date can't be resolved from its digits — infer the document's convention once, don't guess per-field.** When both parts are ≤ 12 (e.g. `05/07/2026`), resolve the order once per document — never per source or per field — in this order. (1) **An unambiguous sibling date fixes the page's convention**: a slash date elsewhere on the same page with a part > 12 (e.g. `24/07/2026`) parses only one way, and a page is almost always internally consistent — read that date's order and apply it to every other slash date on the page. (2) Failing that, **read the declared locale** (``, `og:locale`): default **month-first** (the order `Date` and most JS parsers assume) and flip to day-first only on a *positive* non-US signal — a non-US region in `lang` / `og:locale`, or a non-English language; a bare `en` with unknown region stays month-first. The `.` / `-` separators are day-first regardless. 7 - **When code must react to how a real page actually behaves, investigate it live before you ship — don't deploy a hypothesis you can only test after release.** If a change hinges on the real DOM, computed styles, or runtime state of a page you can't see, hand the user one JavaScript snippet to run in the browser DevTools console and read its output back. Reserve "test it after it's deployed" for behavior you've verified genuinely can't be observed now. 8 - **Make that console request a snippet, not an essay.** Send exactly one code block to paste into the console and ask the user to paste its output back. Skip the prose explaining what you're hoping to learn. 9

1	# Leaflet
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.
4	
5	- **Load Leaflet — and every Leaflet plugin — from a version-pinned CDN URL with a Subresource-Integrity hash and `crossorigin`.** Pin the exact version (`leaflet@1.9.4`, not `@latest`) and carry `integrity="sha256-…"` + `crossorigin=""` on both the CSS `<link>` and the JS `<script>`. The trap is doing this for the core bundle but forgetting a plugin — the one un-pinned `<script>` is the hole.
6	
7	- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A plugin's separate `<script>` (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and add markers straight to the map when it's absent — the base map must still render.
8	
9	- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })`, or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus.
10	
11	- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** The `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve.
12	
13	- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element, clobbering any `transform` you set there on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`.
14

1	# Conversion inventory — every corpus rule, audited
2	
3	> Companion to [../engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) (issue #127). Each discrete instruction in the mounted
4	> corpus, classified by the mechanism that should carry it. This is the audit that answers
5	> "is enough of the corpus convertible?" — and the worklist Phases 1–3 execute against.
6	
7	**Dispositions:**
8	
9	- **check** — post-hoc deterministic check (pack named). *(adv)* = advisory by kind — the
10	  rule's semantics are directional (a smell to judge, not a defect to fix); everything else
11	  ships blocking, fail-fast.
12	- **hook** — PreToolUse gate, blocks before the action runs.
13	- **skill** — becomes an on-demand procedure; unloads from always-on context.
14	- **setting** — platform enforces it (GitHub repo/branch settings); no code at all.
15	- **stays** — process/judgment guidance; remains an instruction. *(judge)* = a deferred
16	  LLM-judge candidate. A whole doc (or a doc's residue after its checks are carved out) that
17	  stays is *delivered* as a skill per DESIGN.md's catalog — same content, harness-managed
18	  trigger instead of an index line the agent must remember to follow.
19	- **knowledge** — platform gotcha; content unchanged, no enforcement possible — delivered as a
20	  `paths`-/description-triggered skill.
21	
22	## Verdict up front
23	
24	~125 discrete instructions audited. **~45 convert to deterministic mechanisms** (≈40 checks
25	across five packs, 4 hooks, 2 settings, plus two whole docs becoming command skills); **~60
26	stay as instructions** (process/judgment) and **~20 are knowledge** — of which roughly half
27	carry a static signature in the artifact and convert into tech-pack checks (Phase 2), the
28	failing check teaching the gotcha at write-time instead of runtime. What genuinely stays no
29	longer means an index soft pointer either: the stays docs and signature-less residues are
30	**delivered as skills** (DESIGN.md's catalog), trading the remembered trigger for a
31	harness-managed one at roughly the same token cost. So: a majority of *instructions* enforced mechanically — no, ~40%. A majority
32	of the **always-loaded context burden** eliminated — yes: four of the five force-loaded docs
33	unload entirely, the two most breakage-prone task docs (filePlacement,
34	textAndFileManipulation) shrink to rationale, and the routing index largely dissolves into
35	skill descriptions. Force-loaded prose that remains: trimmed working-discipline and the
36	engineeringPractices judgment core.
37

39	
40	| Rule | Disposition |
41	|---|---|
42	| working-discipline: problem-first consensus before implementing | stays |
43	| working-discipline: confirm behavior isn't already provided | stays |
44	| working-discipline: misread ≠ wrong artifact; size writing to its idea | stays |

=== packs/node/RULES.md ===
# Node.js

Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.

## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide

Two that recur:

- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.
=== packs/research-project/RULES.md ===
# Research Project Working Procedures — a portable playbook

This document defines **how the owner wants a research project run**, as a
**bootstrap to drop into a new research project** from day one. It is written to
be project-agnostic: it carries the durable working procedures and none of the
subject matter, methods, or results of any particular study.

It is aimed at the recurring class of research it is meant for: **run an
algorithm over a set of similarly-formatted inputs, score it against
user-provided ground truth, and improve the algorithm in repeatable, reviewable
iterations.** Image analysis / computer vision is the archetypal case and the
examples lean that way, but the workflow, ground-truth discipline,
anti-overfitting stance, and session hygiene apply to research work broadly —
read "algorithm", "input", and "render" as whatever they mean for your project.

Treat it as a **default to adapt, not a contract**. When a new project needs a
rule this one doesn't have, add it; when a rule here doesn't fit, say why and
drop it. As you work a real project, replace the generic phrasing with that
project's concrete specifics (its inputs, metrics, invariants) in *that
project's own* docs — keep this bootstrap generic so it stays reusable. The one
non-negotiable is the spirit: **show the work visually, prove each change against
ground truth, never overfit the learning set, and leave the project resumable.**

---

## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step

This is the cadence the owner wants, and it is the **deliverable style**, not
optional polish. Follow it for every substantive algorithmic change.

1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
   it** — do not guess.
2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
   a sensible default and state what you chose.
5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).

### Show, don't just tell
- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.

### Interaction cadence
Keep the owner in the loop with **pictures**, proactively. Ask a question only
when a decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — not to confirm
work you can verify yourself. When you finish a unit of work, leave it committed
and pushed so it can be reviewed or resumed from a fresh session.

---

## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**

- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
  loudly.
- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
  are requirements, not incidental.
- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
  the review overlays.

---

## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set

- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
  in scope.
- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.

---

## 4. Do not overfit the learning set

These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
if it improves a metric.

- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.

---

## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*

Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**

An iteration note captures:
- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
  showed it).
- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
  possible).
- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.

### Definition of done for an accepted change
- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
  changed**.

---

## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path

- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.

---

## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles

When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:

- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.

---

## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations

- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.

---

## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside

- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
    nothing finer.
  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
  mask-free validation path for those sets.
- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
  covered.

---

## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight

- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
  exhausted first.
- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
  warm-up doc.

---

## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner

The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
first-class experiments:

- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
  couldn't.
- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
  the very structure you are measuring.
- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.

---

## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**

When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
substantially change a sub-step.

---

## 13. Continuity across sessions

The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
**resumable** state.

- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
  clean checkout.
- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
  codebase.
- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
  metrics current in it.
- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
  isn't captured yet.
- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.

---

## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)

Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
revived session:

> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
> the research task itself.**
> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted

> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over

> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered

> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
> overwriting.

session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the

# firebase pack

Active when the repo has `firebase.json`. Durable practices for building on Firebase — Firestore
security-rules discipline (merge semantics, server-owned fields, default-deny), callable Cloud
Function patterns (verified-token identity, validation, transactional rate limits, batched
fan-out), testing without live infrastructure (pure-logic extraction, the rules emulator when rules
themselves are under test), and deploy layout (predeploy build hooks, committed project aliases).
Mostly prose — the two mechanical halves of the deploy layout are checks. Earned in
missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (Firestore + Functions + FCM + Google sign-in). Environment
separation and store gating are deliberately NOT here — that is the opt-in
[firebase-release](../firebase-release/README.md) pack.

## Checks

Both are relevance-first: they say nothing until `firebase.json` declares a functions codebase
whose `package.json` is in the checkout, so a rules-only or hosting-only Firebase repo is untouched.

| Rule (≤5 words) | Severity | What |
|---|---|---|
| Functions pin their Node major | blocking | a deployed codebase's `package.json` declares `engines.node` |
| Build script wired as predeploy | blocking | a codebase with a `build` script declares a `predeploy` hook in `firebase.json` |

## Prose (`RULES.md`) — by section

| Section (≤5 words) | How enforced |
|---|---|
| Rules are merge-aware, default-deny | prose (+ the project's rules tests) |
| Functions own identity and limits | prose |
| Test logic pure, rules empirically | prose (+ the project's suites) |
| Deploy layout and aliases | prose + the two checks above |

# the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands
        # outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit; adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ + the other top-level canon code (migrations/, …);
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs-tests/             every canon pack's tests, mirroring packs/
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          node --test "${tests[@]}"
      - name: Conformance sweep
        # The world sweep's home is the test/CI flow (not the Stop hook, which
        # carries only the work scope) — this canon repo models the pattern
        # bootstrap wires into consumers. World only: the work scope judges a
        # session's change and runs at that session's Stop hook, not here.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage (.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/tasks/growth-promote/task.md)
        # is the one change bounded to packs/ + skills/ — an ordinary engine PR legitimately edits
        # checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix
        # (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs

input.body:
Daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` run for 2026-07-28 (dispatched by #504; ledger #450).

## What converted

**`packs/leaflet/RULES.md`** — *"Load Leaflet — and every Leaflet plugin — from a version-pinned CDN URL with a Subresource-Integrity hash and `crossorigin`"* → **`leaflet/asset-integrity`** (blocking).

It passes the check-the-world test cleanly: the thing the rule constrains — the CDN wiring of the assets — is written into the page's own `<script>` / `<link>` tags, a static signature a post-hoc scan sees directly. Nothing about it is in-flight or judgment.

The prose bullet is gone; the failure message owns the rule now (what / why / fix / `doc:` back to `packs/leaflet/RULES.md`).

## Parsed, not grepped

Grepping for `unpkg.com` or for a missing `integrity` answers the wrong question. The rule is about one *tag*, so the scan reads each `<script>`/`<link>`'s own attributes and judges only those:

- only a tag whose **own** `src`/`href` is a **remote** URL naming a Leaflet asset is judged;
- HTML comments are blanked first (newlines kept, so line numbers hold);
- an exact pin means a `major.minor…` reached by the URL's own delimiters (`leaflet@1.9.4/…`, `/leaflet/1.9.4/…`, `leaflet-1.9.4.js`) — `@latest` and a major-only `@1` are not pins;
- the finding names *which* of pin / `integrity` / `crossorigin` is missing, so a half-wired tag gets a precise message.

Quiet by construction: a locally vendored `js/leaflet.js`, a `preconnect` to the CDN host, a non-Leaflet CDN script, a Leaflet URL sitting in page text or in a JS string, and an example written inside an HTML comment.

## See-it-fail

`packs-tests/leaflet/pack.test.mjs` — 6 fixtures:

- **fires**: the plugin `<script>` left bare beside a correctly wired core bundle (the exact trap the prose named), and `@latest` / a version-less URL (asserting the finding names the pin);
- **clean**: core + plugin both pinned and hashed, across unpkg and cdnjs URL shapes;
- **FP guards**: vendored/same-origin asset + preconnect, non-Leaflet CDN tag + Leaflet URL in text and in a JS string, and the HTML-comment case.

Both firing fixtures were verified red with the rule's `run` neutered to `return []`, then the check restored — the four guards and the clean case stayed green throughout, so they prove the scoping rather than the absence of a scan.

## Verification

- Full offline suite (the CI test roots): **786 pass, 0 fail**.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`: **0 blocking, 7 advisory** — the same seven pre-existing `file-placement` advisories on `engine/` that main carries; no new findings.
- The `leaflet` pack is not declared in this repo, so the new rule doesn't run on the canon's own sweep; the fixture test is its proof.

## Considered and deliberately left as prose

- **leaflet: keep the tile provider's attribution + a real `maxZoom`.** A licence term and a genuine static-ish signature, but `attribution` can legitimately be supplied away from the `L.tileLayer(...)` call (`attributionControl.addAttribution`, a shared options constant), so a confident detection isn't available without guessing. Left as prose rather than shipped shaky.
- **leaflet: feature-detect an optional plugin / embedded map defaults to `scrollWheelZoom: false` / `divIcon` transform on an inner span** — runtime and layout-intent behaviours with no artifact signature.
- **html, node** — parser/jsdom divergence knowledge, visible only at runtime.
- **research-project, spec-driven-product, flutter (toolchain, goldens)** — process and judgment, or needing an arbitrary threshold.
- **android, ios, play-store-release** — stubs, no rules captured yet.

Outcome ceiling for this task is `open-pr`: for owner review, **not** to be merged or auto-merged by automation.

Refs #504, #450

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
